title: Protecting Cut Axons Did Not Rescue This ALS Model

scenes.visual: Title card: Protecting Cut Axons Did Not Rescue This ALS Model.

scenes.tts: Why do some neurons fail while their neighbours survive? No one yet knows. So how do you test one idea about it?
scenes.visual: A row of motor neurons; some fade while neighbours stay bright. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Why do some neurons fail while their neighbours survive? No one yet knows. So how do you test one idea about it?

scenes.tts: Start with injury. When an axon is cut, the piece cut off from the cell body breaks into fragments within days.
scenes.visual: A nerve with one axon highlighted. A cut appears; the part beyond the cut breaks into beads. Label: within days.
scenes.narration: Start with injury. When an axon is cut, the piece cut off from the cell body breaks into fragments within days.

scenes.tts: This was long thought of as passive wasting. It is not. The cut-off piece runs an active destruction program.
scenes.visual: A label 'passive wasting' is crossed out and replaced by 'active program'.
scenes.narration: This was long thought of as passive wasting. It is not. The cut-off piece runs an active destruction program.

scenes.tts: In flies and mice, removing one gene, Sarm one, keeps the cut-off piece intact for weeks.
scenes.caption: In flies and mice, removing one gene, Sarm1, keeps the cut-off piece intact for weeks.
scenes.visual: Two mice side by side, each with a cut nerve. Wild type: the cut-off part is beaded. Sarm1-null: the cut-off part is still whole. On screen only: two weeks.
scenes.narration: In flies and mice, removing one gene, Sarm1, keeps the cut-off piece intact for weeks.

scenes.tts: Axons also degenerate in A L S. So the obvious next test is to remove Sarm one from a mouse model of A L S.
scenes.caption: Axons also degenerate in ALS. So the obvious next test is to remove Sarm1 from a mouse model of ALS.
scenes.visual: A spinal cord with motor axons thinning out toward muscle. Label: ALS model. An arrow brings in the Sarm1-null gene card.
scenes.narration: Axons also degenerate in ALS. So the obvious next test is to remove Sarm1 from a mouse model of ALS.

scenes.tts: These mice make a mutant human S O D one protein, and they develop motor neuron disease.
scenes.caption: These mice make a mutant human SOD1 protein, and they develop motor neuron disease.
scenes.visual: Label: SOD1G93A mice, overexpressing mutant human SOD1.
scenes.narration: These mice make a mutant human SOD1 protein, and they develop motor neuron disease.

scenes.tts: Predict. Without Sarm one, will these mice live longer?
scenes.caption: Predict. Without Sarm1, will these mice live longer?
scenes.visual: Empty survival axes: percent alive against age. On screen: Pause. Will removing Sarm1 help?
scenes.narration: Predict. Without Sarm1, will these mice live longer?

scenes.tts: No. Survival did not improve. Nor did the behavioural, nerve recording or tissue measures.
scenes.visual: Two survival curves, with and without Sarm1, close together. Label: schematic, no survival benefit detected. Small icons for behaviour, electrophysiology and histology, each labelled: no benefit detected on the measures tested.
scenes.narration: No. Survival did not improve. Nor did the behavioural, nerve recording or tissue measures.

scenes.tts: Needed after a cut does not mean needed in this disease. The motor neurons may die by another route.
scenes.visual: The Sarm1 card splits in two: needed after a cut (check) and needed in this disease (not shown).
scenes.narration: Needed after a cut does not mean needed in this disease. The motor neurons may die by another route.

scenes.tts: And one mouse model is not human A L S. The result stays inside this model.
scenes.caption: And one mouse model is not human ALS. The result stays inside this model.
scenes.visual: Label beneath the curves: one SOD1 overexpression model, not human ALS.
scenes.narration: And one mouse model is not human ALS. The result stays inside this model.

scenes.tts: Does this show axon loss does not matter in A L S? No. That claim goes too far.
scenes.caption: Does this show axon loss does not matter in ALS? No. That claim goes too far.
scenes.visual: A speech bubble: 'axon degeneration does not matter in ALS', stamped: goes too far.
scenes.narration: Does this show axon loss does not matter in ALS? No. That claim goes too far.

scenes.tts: A better test measures axons, nerve-muscle contacts and cell bodies, as well as survival, in the same mice.
scenes.visual: A checklist builds: axon counts, neuromuscular junctions, motor unit estimates, motor neuron counts, onset and survival.
scenes.narration: A better test measures axons, nerve-muscle contacts and cell bodies, as well as survival, in the same mice.

scenes.tts: The scorers should not know each mouse's genotype. Then the test is repeated in a second model.
scenes.visual: A blindfold icon over the scorer; a second mouse model card labelled TDP-43 model slides in.
scenes.narration: The scorers should not know each mouse's genotype. Then the test is repeated in a second model.

scenes.tts: Here is what each result supports. Losing Sarm one protects cut axons. In this model, losing it did not improve the disease measures.
scenes.caption: Here is what each result supports. Losing Sarm1 protects cut axons. In this model, losing it did not improve the disease measures.
scenes.visual: Three stacked cards: Sarm1 loss protects cut axons (flies and mice); Sarm1 loss did not improve measured outcomes (this SOD1G93A model; need in disease not shown); benefit in human ALS (not tested here).
scenes.narration: Here is what each result supports. Losing Sarm1 protects cut axons. In this model, losing it did not improve the disease measures.

scenes.visual: The cards and arrows hold on screen.

scenes.tts: State what each result supports, and what it leaves open. Then design the next experiment to test what is still open.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: what each result supports; what it leaves open; the next experiment tests what is open.
scenes.narration: State what each result supports, and what it leaves open. Then design the next experiment to test what is still open.
